Genesis.author: Jews and Christians have long received Genesis as the first of the five books of Moses, and many still hold that view [[nabre:thepentateuch/0]] [[bo:18623]]. The book itself does not name its author [[eob:Genesis]].
Genesis.date: If Moses wrote it, in the wilderness after the Exodus: about 1445 BC on the early dating [[bo:18623]], or by 1240 BC at the latest on the later one [[eob:Genesis]].
Genesis.to: The people of Israel, to help them understand their roots in Abraham, Isaac and Jacob [[bo:18623]], and as the groundwork for the rest of the books of Moses [[eob:Genesis]].
Genesis.why: The book of beginnings. God, the good King of all, makes the world and gives people the task of caring for it under him [[bible:Genesis 1:26-28]]. When they turn from him, he promises that a child of the woman will one day crush the serpent [[bible:Genesis 3:15]] [[ks:1]].
Genesis.story: Everything that follows grows from here. God promises Abraham a family, a land and blessing for every nation on earth [[bible:Genesis 12:1-3]], and the rest of the Bible tells how he keeps those promises [[ks:1]]. Genesis ends with the family small and far from home in Egypt, yet kept alive by God’s grace, not by their own goodness [[ks:1]] [[bible:Genesis 50:20]]. Scholars picture the whole Bible as a symphony in four movements, creation, fall, redemption and re-creation: Genesis plays the first two and begins the third, and the Bible’s last chapters return to its garden, river and tree of life [[dl:Genesis]] [[bible:Revelation 22:1-2]].
Genesis.genre: Narrative history, organised under ten headings, “these are the generations of…” (Hebrew toledot, best translated “history”) [[eob:Genesis]] [[bo:18623]].
Genesis.debate: How Genesis was written: many modern scholars see it as woven from older sources (J, E, D and P) given final shape after the exile, a theory others reject [[eob:Genesis]] [[nabre:thepentateuch/0]]; and how its creation and flood accounts compare with other ancient Near Eastern stories, such as the Gilgamesh and Atrahasis epics [[nabre:genesis/6]] [[eob:Genesis]].
Genesis.structureNote: The book falls into two halves, the early history (1–11) and the story of the patriarchs (12–50) [[eob:Genesis]]; the outline below follows the main characters of the text.

Exodus.author: Very early Jewish tradition held that Moses wrote it, and many still hold that view [[eob:Book-Exodus]] [[nabre:thepentateuch/0]]; the book records Moses writing down God’s words [[bible:Exodus 24:4]]. It does not name its author [[eob:Book-Exodus]].
Exodus.date: The events: about 1446 BC on the early dating, or about 1260 BC on the late dating, which links the city of Raamses (1:11) with Pharaoh Rameses II; both are held by evangelical scholars [[ref:esv-exodus-date]]. The evidence is not enough for a final decision, but points to the second half of the second millennium BC [[eob:Book-Exodus]].
Exodus.to: The people of Israel, as the story of how God made them his own nation [[nabre:exodus/0]].
Exodus.why: God rescues his people. He hears Israel’s cry in Egypt, breaks Pharaoh’s power, makes a covenant with them at Mount Sinai, and comes to live among them in the tabernacle [[ks:2]] [[nabre:exodus/0]]. The rescue, the law and the tabernacle all say one thing: God is with his people as their Saviour and King, and the exodus is the greatest act of salvation in the Old Testament [[dl:Exodus]].
Exodus.story: The family promised to Abraham has become a great nation [[bible:Exodus 1:7]]. The book ends with God’s glory filling the tent at the centre of the camp [[bible:Exodus 40:34]] [[ks:2]]. The rescue from slavery becomes the Bible’s great picture of salvation, and the New Testament calls Jesus our Passover lamb [[bible:1 Corinthians 5:7]].
Exodus.genre: About half narrative, the first nineteen chapters, and about half law and instructions for worship [[eob:Book-Exodus]].
Exodus.debate: The date of the Exodus [[ref:esv-exodus-date]]; why no Egyptian king is named and why Egyptian monuments are silent, which is expected since defeats were not recorded [[eob:Book-Exodus]]; how its laws compare with Hammurabi’s code, with which direct parallels are fairly few [[eob:Book-Exodus]]; and whether, as many modern scholars think, it was woven from older sources [[nabre:thepentateuch/0]].
Exodus.structureNote: The NABRE divides the book into eight parts [[nabre:exodus/0]]; the outline below follows them.

Leviticus.author: It presents its laws as given by God through Moses [[bible:Leviticus 26:46]], and many scholars defend that view [[eob:Leviticus]]. The book does not name its author [[eob:Leviticus]].
Leviticus.date: On the traditional view, the time at Sinai, soon after the Exodus [[eob:Leviticus]].
Leviticus.to: The people of Israel and their priests. Its laws are meant to shape the whole way of life of those who hear them [[nabre:leviticus/0]].
Leviticus.why: How can a holy God live among his people? Leviticus answers: he himself provides the way, through sacrifice that covers sin, through cleansing, and through a holy life lived before him [[ks:3]] [[eob:Leviticus]]. Behind every law stands one truth: God is holy, so only those made clean can come near him [[dl:Leviticus]] [[bible:Leviticus 11:45]].
Leviticus.story: It stands at the centre of the five books of Moses [[nabre:leviticus/0]]. Its sacrifices and its priests point forward to Jesus, the great high priest whose one sacrifice brings full forgiveness [[ks:3]] [[bible:Hebrews 9:11-14]]. Its call still stands: be holy, because God is holy [[bible:1 Peter 1:15-16]].
Leviticus.genre: Laws for worship and daily life, with a few short narratives [[nabre:leviticus/0]].
Leviticus.debate: How and when the book was composed: many critical scholars see it as Priestly material finished around 550 BC or later [[eob:Leviticus]] [[nabre:leviticus/0]]; what the verb kipper, “atone”, means: to wipe away, to cover, or to pay a ransom [[eob:Leviticus]]; and whether the Holiness laws came before or after Ezekiel, which cannot be shown with certainty [[eob:Leviticus]].
Leviticus.structureNote: The outline follows the five parts of the NABRE introduction [[nabre:leviticus/0]].

Numbers.author: Like the other books of the Pentateuch, it has traditionally been credited to Moses [[easton:Numbers-Book]]; it says Moses wrote down the list of Israel’s journeys [[bible:Numbers 33:2]].
Numbers.date: The events cover about thirty-eight years, from the second year after the Exodus to the fortieth [[easton:Numbers-Book]] [[nabre:numbers/0]].
Numbers.to: The people of Israel, who were about to enter the land God had promised [[nabre:numbers/0]].
Numbers.why: Israel marches through the wilderness with God at the centre of the camp. A generation that would not trust him dies on the way, yet God does not take back his promise, and a new generation stands ready to enter the land [[ks:4]] [[nabre:numbers/0]]. Even when his people grumble and rebel, God keeps his covenant, guides them and provides for them [[dl:Numbers]].
Numbers.story: Even the hired prophet Balaam is made to bless Israel, and he sees a star and a king rising from Jacob [[bible:Numbers 24:17]], which Christians read as pointing to Christ [[ks:4]]. Hebrews looks back on the wilderness as a warning not to harden our hearts [[bible:Hebrews 3:7-19]].
Numbers.genre: Law and history together, with two censuses, travel lists and the poetic oracles of Balaam [[nabre:numbers/0]].
structure: Rebellion and forty years in the wilderness
A new generation prepares to enter the land
Numbers.debate: How the book was composed, since many modern scholars see the Pentateuch as woven from several sources [[nabre:thepentateuch/0]]; the route through the wilderness, since the list of stages is not complete and many places are not known [[nabre:numbers/33]]; and what exactly Moses’s sin at Meribah was, which the text does not make clear [[nabre:numbers/20]].
Numbers.structureNote: The NABRE divides the book into three parts [[nabre:numbers/0]]; the outline below follows them.

Deuteronomy.author: It is presented as three speeches of Moses [[nabre:deuteronomy/0]], and says Moses wrote this law down [[bible:Deuteronomy 31:9]]. Those who hold that he wrote it point to its likeness to Hittite treaties of the second millennium BC [[tbd:004:Deuteronomy, Book of]]; an editor added the account of his death [[bo:885]].
Deuteronomy.date: If by Moses, the 1300s or 1200s BC [[tbd:004:Deuteronomy, Book of]], or about 1406 BC on the early dating of the Exodus [[bo:885]].
Deuteronomy.to: The new generation of Israel on the plains of Moab, about to enter the promised land [[nabre:deuteronomy/1]] [[tosn:Deuteronomy 4:13]].
Deuteronomy.why: Moses’ last words before Israel enters the land. Love the LORD your God with all your heart [[bible:Deuteronomy 6:5]]: obedience here is a grateful answer to his love, not a way of earning it [[ks:5]].
Deuteronomy.story: Moses looks ahead to Israel’s failure and exile, and beyond it to a day when God will change their hearts himself [[bible:Deuteronomy 30:6]] [[ks:5]]. He also promises a prophet like him [[bible:Deuteronomy 18:15]], fulfilled in Jesus [[bible:Acts 3:22-26]]. Jesus answered every temptation with words from this book [[bible:Matthew 4:4]]. It is one of the Old Testament books the New Testament quotes most, and Moses’ promise of a prophet like him kept Israel watching until John the Baptist and Jesus came [[dl:Deuteronomy]] [[bible:John 1:21]].
Deuteronomy.genre: Speeches of Moses that follow the pattern of an ancient covenant treaty, with laws, blessings and curses [[tbd:004:Deuteronomy, Book of]] [[tosn:Deuteronomy 1:1]].
structure: Third address: covenant renewal and farewell
Deuteronomy.debate: Whether Moses wrote it, or, as many critical scholars hold, it was written in King Josiah’s time or composed over several centuries [[tbd:004:Deuteronomy, Book of]] [[nabre:deuteronomy/0]]; its relation to the book of the law found in the temple in 622 BC [[nabre:deuteronomy/0]]; and how closely it follows Hittite treaty forms [[tbd:004:Deuteronomy, Book of]]. Its Greek name, “second law”, can mislead, since it is not a simple repeat of the law [[tbd:004:Deuteronomy, Book of]].
Deuteronomy.structureNote: The NABRE divides the book into three addresses of Moses and the account of his death [[nabre:deuteronomy/0]]; the outline below follows them.

Joshua.author: The book does not say. The Talmud names Joshua, perhaps because he “wrote these words” of the covenant renewal [[tbd:010:Joshua, Book of]] [[bible:Joshua 24:26]].
Joshua.date: There are no clear markers [[tbd:010:Joshua, Book of]]. A conservative view dates the writing between 1375 and 1045 BC [[tbd:010:Joshua, Book of]].
Joshua.to: Israel, to show how the LORD gave them the land and how they might prosper in it [[tbd:010:Joshua, Book of]], and to warn them against losing it [[nabre:joshua/0]].
Joshua.why: God keeps his word: Israel enters the land promised to Abraham. The victories are the LORD’s, not Israel’s, and the people are called to choose to serve him [[ks:6]] [[bible:Joshua 24:15]].
Joshua.story: A second part of the promise to Abraham comes true [[bible:Joshua 21:43-45]] [[ks:6]]. Joshua’s name means “the LORD saves”, the same name as Jesus [[nabre:numbers/13]]. Hebrews says the rest Joshua gave was a picture of a deeper rest still to come [[bible:Hebrews 4:8-9]]. “Jesus” is simply the Greek form of the name Joshua, and the New Testament sees in Jesus the leader who brings God’s people into their lasting inheritance [[dl:Joshua]].
Joshua.genre: History, the first of the books the Hebrew Bible calls the Former Prophets [[tbd:010:Joshua, Book of]], with lists of tribal lands that preserve older traditions [[nabre:joshua/0]].
Joshua.debate: When and by whom it was written: critical scholars suggest the 600s BC or the exile, as part of a larger history from Deuteronomy to Kings [[tbd:010:Joshua, Book of]] [[nabre:joshua/0]]; how its swift conquest fits Judges 1, which suggests a slower settlement [[nabre:joshua/0]]; and how to read the destruction it describes alongside the New Testament command to love enemies [[nabre:joshua/0]].
Joshua.structureNote: The NABRE divides the book into three parts [[nabre:joshua/0]]; the outline below follows them, with the conquest in two halves.

Judges.author: The book does not name its author. Jewish tradition named Samuel; many scholars think a writer of the early monarchy compiled it from older records [[tbd:010:Judges, Book of]].
Judges.date: The final editing reflects the early days of Israel’s kings [[tbd:010:Judges, Book of]]. The period itself began about 1370–1360 BC on the early dating of the Exodus, or near the end of the 1200s BC on the later one [[tbd:010:Judges, Book of]].
Judges.to: Israel under its first kings, explaining why the tribes did not take all the land and pointing toward a king who would shepherd the people [[tbd:010:Judges, Book of]].
Judges.why: Israel lives in the promised land, yet keeps forgetting God. Again and again they turn to idols, cry out, and are rescued by a judge God sends [[bible:Judges 2:16-19]], showing his patience with a stubborn people [[ks:7]].
Judges.story: The book ends in chaos: there was no king, and everyone did what was right in their own eyes [[bible:Judges 21:25]]. It leaves us longing for a good king, a longing met in David and finally in Jesus [[ks:7]]. For all their flaws, Gideon, Barak, Samson and Jephthah are remembered for their faith [[bible:Hebrews 11:32-34]], and their story shows how much God’s people need a champion to fight for them [[dl:Judges]].
Judges.genre: Hero stories of twelve judges from different regions, framed by an introduction and two closing stories [[tbd:010:Judges, Book of]] [[tosn:Judges 17:1-21:25]].
structure: Everyone did what was right in his own eyes
Judges.debate: How long the period of the judges lasted, which depends on the date of the Exodus [[tbd:010:Judges, Book of]]; and whether the book argues for David’s rule rather than Saul’s, as some scholars think [[tbd:010:Judges, Book of]].
Judges.structureNote: The outline follows the book’s introduction, the stories of the judges and its two closing stories [[tbd:010:Judges, Book of]].

Ruth.author: Unknown [[tbd:018:Ruth, Book of]]. Since it closes with David’s family line, it was probably written after David began to reign, perhaps by someone close to him such as Samuel, Nathan or Abiathar [[tbd:018:Ruth, Book of]].
Ruth.date: The events took place around 1100 BC, in the days of the judges [[tosn:Ruth 1:1]]. It was likely written after David became king [[tbd:018:Ruth, Book of]].
Ruth.to: Israel, perhaps to show that David’s family was the chosen royal line, and to explain how a faithful Moabite woman became part of Israel [[tbd:018:Ruth, Book of]].
Ruth.why: A quiet story of loyal love in a dark time. A foreign widow trusts Israel’s God, and through the kindness of Boaz, God works unseen to bring hope out of loss [[ks:8]] [[bible:Ruth 2:12]]. God is seldom mentioned by the narrator, yet his hidden care shapes every turn of the story [[dl:Ruth]].
Ruth.story: Ruth becomes the great-grandmother of King David [[bible:Ruth 4:17]], the answer to Judges’ cry for a king [[ks:8]]. She is named in Jesus’ family tree [[bible:Matthew 1:5]], a sign that God’s blessing was always meant for all nations [[ks:8]].
Ruth.genre: A short story that ends with a family line of ten generations, from Perez to David [[tosn:Ruth 4:18-22]].
Ruth.debate: When it was written, which affects what its purpose was [[tbd:018:Ruth, Book of]].

1 Samuel.author: Unknown. It cannot have been Samuel alone, since his death is reported in 25:1 [[tbd:019:Samuel, Books of First and Second]]. Some suggest Samuel with the prophets Nathan and Gad (1 Chronicles 29:29), but the real author cannot be determined [[tbd:019:Samuel, Books of First and Second]].
1 Samuel.date: Its final form comes some time after Solomon’s death and the division of the kingdom in 930 BC [[tbd:019:Samuel, Books of First and Second]].
1 Samuel.to: Israel, about what kind of king fits God’s covenant [[tbd:019:Samuel, Books of First and Second]].
1 Samuel.why: God gives Israel a king. Hannah sings that God lifts up the humble and brings down the proud [[bible:1 Samuel 2:7-8]], and that is the story of Saul, who turns from God, and young David, a man after God’s own heart [[ks:9]] [[bible:1 Samuel 13:14]].
1 Samuel.story: God looks at the heart, not the outside [[bible:1 Samuel 16:7]]. Hannah’s song already looks ahead to God’s anointed king [[bible:1 Samuel 2:10]], and the line of kings that begins here leads to Jesus [[tbd:019:Samuel, Books of First and Second]] [[ks:9]]. The young shepherd who risked his life for his sheep [[bible:1 Samuel 17:34-35]] points ahead to the good shepherd who lays down his life for his [[dl:Samuel]] [[bible:John 10:11]].
1 Samuel.genre: Historical narrative with poetry, such as Hannah’s song (2:1–10) [[tbd:019:Samuel, Books of First and Second]]. 1 and 2 Samuel were one book until the Greek translators split them in two [[tbd:019:Samuel, Books of First and Second]].
1 Samuel.debate: Who wrote it, and how its mixed feelings about kingship fit together; the book resolves them in chapter 12 [[tbd:019:Samuel, Books of First and Second]].

2 Samuel.author: Unknown. 1 and 2 Samuel were originally one book, and its real author cannot be determined [[tbd:019:Samuel, Books of First and Second]].
2 Samuel.date: David ruled the strongest kingdom of the region about 1000 BC [[tbd:004:David]]. The book reached its final form some time after the kingdom split in 930 BC [[tbd:019:Samuel, Books of First and Second]].
2 Samuel.to: Israel, about David’s reign and what kind of king fits God’s covenant [[tbd:019:Samuel, Books of First and Second]].
2 Samuel.why: David reigns, and God makes him a promise: his family will rule forever [[bible:2 Samuel 7:12-16]]. David’s great failure with Bathsheba shows that even the best king is not the final answer [[ks:9]].
2 Samuel.story: The promise to David becomes the heart of Israel’s hope for a Messiah [[ks:9]], fulfilled in the eternal reign of Jesus Christ [[tosn:2 Samuel 7:19]] [[bible:Luke 1:32-33]].
2 Samuel.genre: Historical narrative with poetry, such as David’s laments and his song in chapter 22 [[tbd:019:Samuel, Books of First and Second]]. Chapters 21–24 are arranged by topic, not by time [[tosn:2 Samuel 21:1–24:25]].
2 Samuel.debate: Who wrote it and when it took its final form [[tbd:019:Samuel, Books of First and Second]].

1 Kings.author: Unknown; the book is anonymous [[tbd:011:Kings, Books of First and Second]]. Jewish tradition in the Talmud names Jeremiah, and an origin among the prophets fits the evidence well [[tbd:011:Kings, Books of First and Second]]. It draws on official royal annals, “the chronicles of the kings” [[tbd:011:Kings, Books of First and Second]].
1 Kings.date: The events run from Solomon’s accession to the divided kingdoms [[tbd:011:Kings, Books of First and Second]]; Solomon’s fourth year was about 967 BC [[tosn:1 Kings 6:1]] and the kingdom split under Rehoboam in 931 BC [[tosn:1 Kings 12:1]]. 1 and 2 Kings were completed in exile, likely between 561 and 539 BC [[tbd:011:Kings, Books of First and Second]].
1 Kings.to: The exiles, who were asking how and why Jerusalem and the temple could fall [[tbd:011:Kings, Books of First and Second]].
1 Kings.why: Solomon’s reign shines like a return to paradise, with wisdom, peace and the temple filled with God’s glory [[bible:1 Kings 8:10-11]]. Then his heart turns to other gods, and the kingdom splits in two [[ks:10]].
1 Kings.story: Through it all God’s word proves true: what his prophets say comes to pass [[ks:10]] [[tbd:011:Kings, Books of First and Second]]. Elijah’s stand on Mount Carmel shows that the LORD alone is God [[bible:1 Kings 18:39]]. Jesus is the greater king, wiser than Solomon [[bible:Matthew 12:42]]. Through all the turmoil, a son of David stays on the throne in Jerusalem for about three and a half centuries, which is why the Gospels take such care to show that Jesus is the Son of David [[dl:Kings]].
1 Kings.genre: History written for theological reasons, not a modern history textbook [[tbd:011:Kings, Books of First and Second]].
1 Kings.debate: Who compiled it, and how the dates given for the kings of Israel and Judah fit together into one timeline [[tbd:011:Kings, Books of First and Second]].

2 Kings.author: Unknown; 1 and 2 Kings are anonymous [[tbd:011:Kings, Books of First and Second]]. Jewish tradition names Jeremiah, and an origin among the prophets fits the evidence well [[tbd:011:Kings, Books of First and Second]].
2 Kings.date: It covers the divided kingdoms, the fall of Samaria in 722 BC [[tosn:2 Kings 17:5–6]], Jerusalem’s fall in 586 BC, and Jehoiachin’s release about 561 BC [[tbd:011:Kings, Books of First and Second]]. Written in exile, likely between 561 and 539 BC [[tbd:011:Kings, Books of First and Second]].
2 Kings.to: The exiles, asking how and why the temple and David’s throne had fallen [[tbd:011:Kings, Books of First and Second]].
2 Kings.why: Both kingdoms walk away from God, and both go into exile, Israel to Assyria and Judah to Babylon [[bible:2 Kings 17:7]] [[bible:2 Kings 25:21]]. God’s warnings were patient, and his word came true [[ks:10]]. The book is written for people in exile, to explain why it happened and to show that God had not given up on David’s line [[dl:Kings]].
2 Kings.story: The book ends with a quiet hope: David’s heir is released from prison in Babylon [[bible:2 Kings 25:27-30]]. God had promised David a lamp that would not go out [[bible:2 Kings 8:19]], and he had not forgotten [[ks:10]].
2 Kings.genre: History written for theological reasons, drawing on royal annals [[tbd:011:Kings, Books of First and Second]].
2 Kings.debate: How the reigns of the kings fit into one timeline, and how the book compares with Assyrian and Babylonian records [[tosn:2 Kings 17:5–6]] [[tbd:011:Kings, Books of First and Second]].

1 Chronicles.author: Unknown, usually called “the Chronicler” [[tbd:003:Chronicles, Books of First and Second]]. The Talmud says Ezra wrote it, and many scholars agree, but there is no general agreement [[tbd:003:Chronicles, Books of First and Second]].
1 Chronicles.date: Probably around 400 BC, in the Persian period [[tbd:003:Chronicles, Books of First and Second]].
1 Chronicles.to: Jews living in Jerusalem under Persian rule after the exile [[tbd:003:Chronicles, Books of First and Second]].
1 Chronicles.why: Israel’s story retold for the people back from exile, to give them hope. From Adam to David, it shows that God’s promise to David still stands and that worship of God belongs at the centre of life [[ks:11]] [[tbd:003:Chronicles, Books of First and Second]].
1 Chronicles.story: It is fundamentally a book of hope: though there was no king on the throne, God’s kingdom would still come [[ks:11]]. God’s promise to David here [[bible:1 Chronicles 17:11-14]] looks ahead to the Son of David who reigns forever [[bible:Luke 1:32-33]].
1 Chronicles.genre: Genealogies (chapters 1–9) and the reign of David (chapters 10–29) [[tbd:003:Chronicles, Books of First and Second]].
1 Chronicles.debate: Who wrote it and when, and whether the same author wrote Ezra and Nehemiah [[tbd:003:Chronicles, Books of First and Second]].

2 Chronicles.author: Unknown, usually called “the Chronicler”; the Talmud names Ezra, but there is no general agreement [[tbd:003:Chronicles, Books of First and Second]].
2 Chronicles.date: Probably around 400 BC, in the Persian period [[tbd:003:Chronicles, Books of First and Second]].
2 Chronicles.to: Jews in Jerusalem under Persian rule, for whom temple worship mattered greatly [[tbd:003:Chronicles, Books of First and Second]].
2 Chronicles.why: Solomon builds the temple, and the kings of Judah rise or fall by whether they seek the LORD. Whenever a king humbles himself and prays, God hears [[bible:2 Chronicles 7:14]] [[ks:11]].
2 Chronicles.story: It ends not with ruin but with an invitation: King Cyrus lets God’s people go up to Jerusalem [[bible:2 Chronicles 36:23]]. In the Hebrew Bible it is the last book, so the Old Testament ends looking forward [[tbd:003:Chronicles, Books of First and Second]] [[ks:11]].
2 Chronicles.genre: History drawing on earlier records, retelling Samuel and Kings with its own concerns [[tbd:003:Chronicles, Books of First and Second]].
2 Chronicles.debate: Who wrote it and when, and whether its author also wrote Ezra and Nehemiah [[tbd:003:Chronicles, Books of First and Second]].

Ezra.author: Many believe Ezra himself collected and wrote the material; parts are told in his own words [[tbd:002:Book of Ezra]].
Ezra.date: The events run from Cyrus’s decree after he took Babylon in 539 BC to Ezra’s work under Artaxerxes I (465–424 BC) [[tbd:002:Book of Ezra]]. Ezra came about 13 years before Nehemiah, who arrived in 445 BC [[tbd:002:Book of Ezra]].
Ezra.to: The Jews who returned from exile under Persian rule [[tbd:002:Book of Ezra]].
Ezra.why: God keeps his promise to bring his people home. He moves a Persian king to let them return [[tosn:Ezra 1:1]], the temple is rebuilt, and Ezra sets his heart to study, live and teach God’s law [[bible:Ezra 7:10]] [[ks:12]]. In Ezra and Nehemiah the whole community, not just its leaders, rebuilds and turns back to the LORD together [[dl:Ezra-Nehemiah]].
Ezra.story: Home again, but not yet free: the people are still under foreign kings and still struggle with sin [[bible:Ezra 9:9]] [[ks:12]]. The return shows God is faithful, while making clear that a deeper rescue is still needed [[ks:12]].
Ezra.genre: History with official letters written in Aramaic and a first-person account by Ezra [[tbd:002:Book of Ezra]].
structure: The first return and the temple
Ezra.debate: Whether Ezra came before Nehemiah [[tbd:002:Book of Nehemiah]], and how to understand the divorces of chapter 10, for which the law gave no clear instructions [[tosn:Ezra 10:4]].

Nehemiah.author: Nehemiah tells much of it in his own words [[bible:Nehemiah 1:1]]. Ezra and Nehemiah formed one book in the early Hebrew Bible [[tbd:002:Book of Nehemiah]].
Nehemiah.date: Nehemiah came to Jerusalem in 445 BC, under Artaxerxes I [[tbd:002:Book of Nehemiah]].
Nehemiah.to: The Jews who had returned to Judah under Persian rule [[tbd:002:Book of Nehemiah]].
Nehemiah.why: A man of prayer leads God’s people to rebuild Jerusalem’s walls in fifty-two days [[bible:Nehemiah 6:15-16]], and the people gather to hear God’s word and renew their promise to him [[bible:Nehemiah 8:8]] [[ks:12]].
Nehemiah.story: It closes the Old Testament history with the people back in the land but still weak and still failing [[ks:12]] [[bible:Nehemiah 13:10-11]]. The longing for a new heart and a true king carries over into the prophets and the Gospels [[ks:12]]. Its honest last chapter, with the old sins creeping back, leaves a question hanging: will God’s people only repeat the past [[dl:Ezra-Nehemiah]]? Only a new heart can answer it [[bible:Jeremiah 31:33]].
Nehemiah.genre: First-person memoir with lists and a covenant ceremony [[bible:Nehemiah 7:5]] [[bible:Nehemiah 9:38]].
Nehemiah.debate: The exact order of Ezra’s and Nehemiah’s work; the book’s message is clear either way [[tbd:002:Book of Nehemiah]].

Esther.author: Unknown. Esther 9:20 says Mordecai “wrote these things”, which may mean he wrote part or all of it [[tbd:002:Book of Esther]].
Esther.date: Set under Xerxes, who died in 465 BC [[tbd:002:Book of Esther]]. When it was written is uncertain: some say shortly after 465 BC, others much later [[tbd:002:Book of Esther]].
Esther.to: Jews living in the Persian empire, and to explain the feast of Purim [[bible:Esther 9:26-28]].
Esther.why: God is never named, yet he is everywhere in this story. Through a brave queen and a string of surprising reversals, he saves his people from a plot to wipe them out [[ks:13]] [[bible:Esther 4:14]].
Esther.story: No plan to destroy God’s people can succeed, because God keeps his covenant [[ks:13]]. The feast of Purim celebrates how sorrow was turned into joy [[bible:Esther 9:22]], and the story shows God’s hand guiding ordinary events [[tosn:Esther 7:9]]. For Christian readers, more was at stake than one nation’s survival: through this people the promised Messiah would come, and God was steering history toward him [[dl:Esther]].
Esther.genre: A court story written by someone who knew Persian court life well [[tbd:002:Book of Esther]].
Esther.debate: When and why it was written, and the extra passages in the Greek version [[tbd:002:Book of Esther]] [[tbd:005:Esther, Additions to]].

Psalms.author: Many writers. The Hebrew titles credit David with 73 psalms, Asaph with 12 and the sons of Korah with 11, Solomon with two, and Moses and Ethan with one each [[tbd:016:Psalms, Book of]]. The titles were added early and are a reasonably reliable guide [[tbd:016:Psalms, Book of]].
Psalms.date: From David’s time, around 1000 BC [[tbd:004:David]], to after the exile [[tosn:Psalm 126:1–6]]. The collection was complete before the Greek translation at the end of the 200s BC [[tbd:016:Psalms, Book of]].
Psalms.to: God’s people at worship, in every situation of life [[tbd:016:Psalms, Book of]].
Psalms.why: The prayer book and songbook of God’s people, with every human feeling brought before God [[tbd:016:Psalms, Book of]]. Its great message is that the LORD reigns [[bible:Psalm 93:1]], so the whole book moves toward praise [[ks:15]]. Joy is its strongest note, and it is quoted in the New Testament more than any other Old Testament book [[dl:Psalms]] [[gbp:4]].
Psalms.story: The five books of Psalms move from David’s reign, through the grief of exile, to the hope of a new David [[ks:15]]. Jesus and the apostles often use the Psalms to show who he is [[tosn:Psalm 1:1–6]], and the book ends with everything that has breath praising the LORD [[bible:Psalm 150:6]].
Psalms.genre: Poetry in five books (1–41, 42–72, 73–89, 90–106, 107–150), perhaps echoing the five books of Moses, each of the first four ending with a doxology [[tbd:016:Psalms, Book of]].
Psalms.debate: What the titles mean: “of David” usually means by David, but with groups it may mean from their collection [[tbd:016:Psalms, Book of]].
